title: Inter-process communication
scopeHtml: Scope: pipes, sockets, shared memory, signals, how to choose, and Linux debugging tools.

notes.title: Why processes need IPC
notes.html:
Processes are isolated on purpose, so to cooperate they need Inter-Process Communication (IPC): a controlled channel the kernel provides. Two families:

  • Message passing: data is copied through the kernel (pipes, sockets, message queues). Safe and simple.
  • Shared memory: both processes map the same physical pages. Fastest, but you must synchronise yourself.

Pick by: same machine or not, throughput, latency, need for a byte stream versus messages, who is allowed to connect, and how failure is detected.

Mechanism Same host only Direction Typical cost Good for
Pipe Yes One way Copy x2 Shell pipelines, parent-child
Named pipe (FIFO) Yes One way Copy x2 Unrelated local processes
Unix domain socket Yes Two way Copy x2 Local services (Docker, Postgres, Nginx to PHP-FPM)
TCP socket No Two way Copy + network stack Anything across machines
Shared memory Yes Both Zero copy High throughput
Signals Yes Notification only Tiny Stop, reload, kill 
# What IPC objects exist on this box
ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd           # pipes show as pipe:[12345], sockets as socket:[...]
ss -xp                         # unix sockets
ipcs                           # SysV shared memory, queues, semaphores
ls /dev/shm                    # POSIX shared memory files

Worked example. Postgres on the same host: connecting through the Unix socket /var/run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432 instead of 127.0.0.1:5432 skips the TCP/IP stack and typically shaves a few tens of microseconds per round trip, which matters for thousands of tiny queries.

Industry examples. Chrome uses Mojo (pipes and shared memory) between browser and renderer processes; Android Binder is a kernel IPC mechanism behind every system service call; Docker's CLI talks to the daemon over /var/run/docker.sock.

Everyday analogy. Neighbours cannot walk into each other's flats: they pass notes through a letter box (messages) or agree to share one whiteboard in the hallway (shared memory).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying shared memory needs no kernel: it needs the kernel to set up the mapping, then no copies.
  • Forgetting message passing is slower for big data because of copies and syscalls.

notes.title: Pipes
notes.html:
A pipe is a kernel buffer with a write end and a read end. Bytes written in come out in the same order. pipe(fds) returns two file descriptors. The default capacity on Linux is 64 KB (16 pages), adjustable with fcntl(F_SETPIPE_SZ) up to /proc/sys/fs/pipe-max-size (1 MB default).

Semantics:

  • Reader blocks when empty; writer blocks when full (this is backpressure, free flow control).
  • Writer closes and buffer empty means reader sees EOF (read returns 0).
  • All readers closed means writer gets SIGPIPE / EPIPE.
  • Writes up to PIPE_BUF (4096 bytes on Linux) are atomic, so concurrent writers do not interleave small lines.

cmd1 | cmd2 is exactly this: the shell makes a pipe, forks twice, wires stdout of the first to the write end and stdin of the second to the read end (dup2), then execs.

import os
r, w = os.pipe()
if os.fork() == 0:           # child reads
    os.close(w)
    print(os.read(r, 100))
    os._exit(0)
os.close(r)                  # parent writes
os.write(w, b"hello")
os.close(w)
os.wait()

Named pipes (FIFOs): mkfifo /tmp/q makes a pipe with a path so unrelated processes can use it.

Production patterns. A deadlock: the parent writes a lot to a child's stdin and waits for it to finish, but the child's stdout pipe fills (64 KB) because the parent is not reading it; both block forever. Subprocess libraries warn about this (use communicate() in Python, read stdout and stderr in separate threads in Java ProcessBuilder). Check with ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd and cat /proc/<pid>/stack / wchan showing pipe_write.

Everyday analogy. A water pipe: fill it faster than it drains and the tap has to wait.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing pipes are two-way. Use two pipes or a socketpair.
  • Forgetting to close unused ends, which prevents EOF and hangs the reader.

notes.title: Sockets
notes.html:
A socket is a two-way communication endpoint addressed by name, used for both local and network IPC. Same API (socket, bind, listen, accept, connect, send, recv) for:

  • TCP (AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM): reliable byte stream across hosts.
  • UDP (SOCK_DGRAM): unreliable datagrams.
  • Unix domain (AF_UNIX): local only, addressed by a file path, can pass file descriptors and verify the peer's UID (SO_PEERCRED). Faster than loopback TCP.

Server steps:

socket() -> bind(addr) -> listen(backlog) -> accept() -> read/write -> close
Client:  socket() -> connect(addr) -> write/read -> close

Each socket has kernel send and receive buffers (SO_SNDBUF, SO_RCVBUF; defaults of a few hundred KB, auto-tuned). A full send buffer blocks (or returns EAGAIN in non-blocking mode). The listen backlog (somaxconn, 4096 default on recent kernels) bounds queued handshakes; overflowing it drops connections: look at ss -lnt (Recv-Q on a listener is the accept queue) and nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows.

$ ss -tnp state established '( sport = :8080 )' | head -3
Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port  Process
0      0      10.0.1.5:8080       10.0.2.9:51022     users:(("java",pid=4410,fd=87))
$ ss -s
Total: 1204
TCP:   1100 (estab 900, closed 150, orphaned 3, timewait 140)

Handling many sockets: one thread per connection, or non-blocking with epoll (epoll_create, epoll_ctl, epoll_wait) so a single thread watches tens of thousands. Edge vs level triggered is a favourite detail: edge-triggered tells you only on new data, so you must read until EAGAIN.

Production incidents. "Too many open files": each socket uses a file descriptor; limit ulimit -n (often 1024 by default; raise to 65535+ via systemd LimitNOFILE). Lots of TIME_WAIT after rapid short connections: use keep-alive and pooling. CLOSE_WAIT piling up means the app forgot to close().

Industry examples. Nginx, Redis and Node.js all rest on epoll; Envoy and HAProxy hold hundreds of thousands of sockets per box; Docker, systemd and Postgres use Unix sockets locally.

Everyday analogy. Telephone: the number is the address, you dial (connect), the other side picks up (accept), and both can talk.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing TCP stream semantics with message boundaries: recv may return half a message; you need framing (length prefix).
  • Raising a thread pool to fix socket exhaustion instead of the fd limit.

notes.title: Shared memory
notes.html:
Shared memory maps the same physical pages into two or more processes' address spaces. After setup no syscall or copy is needed to exchange data. It is the fastest IPC (memory speed, GB/s) but offers no synchronisation or protection: the programmers must add it.

APIs:

  • POSIX: shm_open("/name", ...) creates an object under /dev/shm (a tmpfs), ftruncate sets its size, mmap(MAP_SHARED) maps it.
  • SysV: shmget/shmat (older, see ipcs -m).
  • mmap of a regular file with MAP_SHARED also shares memory between processes and persists to disk.
  • Anonymous shared mapping before fork shares with children.

Synchronise with process-shared mutexes or semaphores (pthread_mutexattr_setpshared, sem_open), futexes, or atomics with a lock-free ring buffer. Without it you get races and torn reads.

Process A virtual 0x7f10... -+
                              +--> same physical frames
Process B virtual 0x7e22... -+

Worked example. Moving 1 GB between processes through a socket needs about 2 copies (user to kernel, kernel to user) plus syscalls, roughly 0.5 to 1 s; via shared memory it is zero copies after mapping, with only a small control message per batch. That is why trading systems, video pipelines and databases use it.

Industry examples. Postgres keeps shared_buffers (commonly 25% of RAM) in shared memory used by all backend processes. Chrome shares large buffers (images, GPU frames) between processes. Android ashmem / memfd share graphics buffers. Aeron and LMAX use shared-memory ring buffers for microsecond messaging.

Failure pitfalls. Leaked segments survive process death: ls /dev/shm, ipcrm. Docker defaults /dev/shm to 64 MB, which crashes Chrome headless and Postgres under load; use --shm-size=1g. Shared memory counts toward the cgroup memory limit.

Everyday analogy. A whiteboard in a shared office: instant for everyone, but two people writing at once makes a mess unless they take turns with a marker (lock).

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming it needs no synchronisation.
  • Storing raw pointers in shared memory; each process maps at a different address, use offsets.

notes.title: Signals
notes.html:
A signal is a small asynchronous notification the kernel delivers to a process: "something happened". It carries a number, not data. The process either runs a handler, ignores it, or takes the default action (terminate, core dump, stop, ignore).

Key signals:

Signal Number Meaning Catchable
SIGHUP 1 Terminal closed; daemons reload config Yes
SIGINT 2 Ctrl-C Yes
SIGQUIT 3 Quit with core/thread dump (JVM prints thread dump) Yes
SIGKILL 9 Kill immediately No
SIGSEGV 11 Bad memory access Yes (rarely wise)
SIGPIPE 13 Write to a pipe with no reader Yes
SIGTERM 15 Polite request to exit (default for kill) Yes
SIGCHLD 17 Child exited Yes
SIGSTOP/SIGCONT 19/18 Pause / resume STOP no
SIGUSR1/2 10/12 App-defined Yes 
kill -TERM 4410         # graceful stop
kill -HUP $(cat /run/nginx.pid)   # reload config without dropping connections
kill -QUIT <jvm-pid>    # thread dump to stdout
kill -9 4410            # last resort

Graceful shutdown pattern in a service (Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds, default 30 s, then SIGKILL):

import signal, sys
def stop(signum, frame):
    # stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, flush, then exit
    sys.exit(0)
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, stop)

Subtleties: handlers must be async-signal-safe (no malloc, no printf; usually just set a flag or write a byte to a self-pipe). Signals interrupt syscalls (EINTR). Standard signals do not queue (several SIGCHLD may merge into one, so loop on waitpid(WNOHANG)). In multithreaded programs, delivery goes to any thread that does not block it; dedicate a thread with sigwait.

Production incident. Container exits with code 137 = 128 + 9: killed by SIGKILL, often the OOM killer or a grace period timeout. 143 = 128 + 15 = SIGTERM. App as shell script (CMD ./start.sh) does not forward SIGTERM to the Java child, so the pod is always force-killed after 30 s; use exec java ... in the script.

Everyday analogy. A tap on the shoulder: no message, just "pay attention". You may react, ignore, or (for SIGKILL) get carried out.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying you can catch SIGKILL.
  • Doing heavy work inside a signal handler.
  • Not knowing the difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL in rolling deploys.

notes.title: Choosing an IPC mechanism
notes.html:
Choose by the questions: do they share a host, how big is the data, how fast must it be, and what must survive a crash?

Decision guide:

  • Parent and child, simple stream: pipe.
  • Local services, request/response, need peer credentials: Unix domain socket (the default sane choice).
  • Might move to another machine later or microservices: TCP/gRPC/HTTP (network sockets; latency about 50 to 500 microseconds on LAN vs under 20 microseconds on a Unix socket).
  • Bulk data or microsecond latency on one host: shared memory + a small signalling channel.
  • Just "stop / reload / ping": signals.
  • Durable, decoupled, many consumers: a message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ) is IPC at system scale.

Decision gravity. Starting with sockets (even local) is a reversible, flexible choice: the same code runs across hosts. Shared memory couples processes tightly and is a harder-to-undo design. Android Binder gives each call a security identity, which is why apps use it over raw sockets.

Debug toolbox.

  • lsof -p <pid>, ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd: what is open.
  • ss -tnlp, ss -xlp: listeners and Unix sockets with owners.
  • strace -f -e trace=network,read,write -p <pid>: what it sends.
  • tcpdump -i lo port 8080: loopback traffic.

Everyday analogy. Delivering a message: shout across the room (signal), pass a note (pipe), phone call (socket), shared whiteboard (shared memory), post office (broker).

Common interview traps.

  • Picking shared memory first because it is "fastest" without a measured need.
  • Ignoring failure detection: with a pipe or socket the peer's death shows up as EOF or reset; with shared memory you must add heartbeats.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• IPC exists because processes are isolated: use message passing (copies, safe) or shared memory (zero copy, you synchronise).
  • Pipes: one-way kernel buffer (64 KB), blocking gives backpressure; EOF when writers close; deadlock if nobody drains stdout.
  • Sockets: two-way, TCP across hosts, Unix domain locally; know the backlog, fd limit, epoll, TIME_WAIT/CLOSE_WAIT.
  • Shared memory (shm_open + mmap): fastest; needs mutexes or lock-free rings; mind /dev/shm size in Docker and leaked segments.
  • Signals: notifications only; SIGTERM graceful, SIGKILL not catchable; exit 137 = SIGKILL, 143 = SIGTERM; handlers must be async-signal-safe.
  • Prefer Unix sockets locally and TCP/gRPC across hosts; use shared memory only with a measured need.

questions.promptHtml: What is a pipe, and what happens when the writer is faster than the reader, or when one end is closed?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know that a pipe is a bounded kernel buffer with blocking semantics, not just a shell symbol.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A pipe is a kernel buffer, 64 KB by default on Linux, with a write fd and a read fd. Bytes come out in the order they went in. If the buffer is full the writer blocks, which is free backpressure. If the buffer is empty the reader blocks. When every writer closes, the reader gets EOF (read returns 0). When every reader closes, the writer gets SIGPIPE or EPIPE.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
pipe(fds) gives fds[0] (read) and fds[1] (write). The data never touches disk; it is copied user to kernel on write and kernel to user on read, so two copies. Because it is a byte stream there are no message boundaries, except that writes of at most PIPE_BUF (4096 bytes on Linux) are atomic, so concurrent writers of short lines do not interleave.

ps aux | grep java | wc -l is the shell creating two pipes, forking three children, and using dup2 to wire stdout of one to the write end and stdin of the next to the read end.

writer --> [ kernel ring buffer, 16 pages = 64 KB ] --> reader
 full  => writer sleeps (pipe_write)     empty => reader sleeps (pipe_read)
 all writers closed => read() returns 0 (EOF)
 all readers closed => write() raises SIGPIPE / EPIPE

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import os
r, w = os.pipe()
if os.fork() == 0:
    os.close(w)              # child must close the unused write end or it never sees EOF
    print(os.read(r, 100))
    os._exit(0)
os.close(r)
os.write(w, b"hello")
os.close(w)
os.wait()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking pipes are two-way. They are not; use two pipes or a socketpair.
  • Not closing the unused ends. A forked child that keeps the write end open means the reader never gets EOF and hangs.
  • Assuming a read returns one whole "message". It returns whatever bytes are available.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a named pipe? -> mkfifo creates a pipe with a filesystem path so unrelated processes can open it; semantics are otherwise identical.
  2. Why does yes | head -1 terminate? -> head exits, the last reader closes, yes gets SIGPIPE and dies.
  3. How do you enlarge the buffer? -> fcntl(fd, F_SETPIPE_SZ, n) up to /proc/sys/fs/pipe-max-size (1 MB default; verify on your kernel).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "one-way channel between processes". The senior adds the 64 KB bound and the backpressure it gives, EOF and SIGPIPE rules, PIPE_BUF atomicity, and the fd-closing discipline that causes most real hangs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Log shippers reading a child's stdout through a pipe stall the producing app when the shipper is slow, because the pipe is full and write to stdout blocks.

questions.promptHtml: Why do processes need IPC at all, and what is the difference between message passing and shared memory?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand isolation and the real trade-off (copies vs synchronisation) before naming mechanisms.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Processes have separate address spaces on purpose, so they cannot touch each other's memory. IPC is a controlled channel the kernel provides. Message passing (pipes, sockets, queues) copies data through the kernel: simple and safe, but each message costs syscalls and copies. Shared memory maps the same physical pages into both processes: no copies after setup and the fastest option, but I must synchronise myself.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Message passing: sender write copies bytes into a kernel buffer, receiver read copies them out. The kernel gives ordering, blocking and failure signals (EOF, reset) for free. Cost is two copies plus two syscalls per message.

Shared memory: the kernel sets up page-table entries so that two virtual ranges point to the same frames. After that, loads and stores go at memory speed (GB/s). The kernel provides no locking and no notification, so I need process-shared mutexes/semaphores, futexes, or a lock-free ring buffer with atomics, plus a heartbeat to detect a dead peer.

Message passing:  A --copy--> [kernel buffer] --copy--> B
Shared memory:    A virt 0x7f10.. --+
                                    +--> same physical frames
                  B virt 0x7e22.. --+
Message passing Shared memory
Copies 2 per message 0 after setup
Sync Kernel provides You provide
Failure detection EOF / reset Heartbeat needed
Cross-host Sockets yes No

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying shared memory involves no kernel. The kernel creates the mapping once.
  • Choosing shared memory "because it is fastest" with no measured need.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is shared memory worth it? -> Bulk data or microsecond latency on one host: Postgres shared buffers, video/GPU frames, trading ring buffers.
  2. Can message passing go across machines? -> Yes with TCP sockets; shared memory cannot.
  3. What does Docker's 64 MB /dev/shm default break? -> Chrome headless and Postgres parallel queries crash; use --shm-size.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "shared memory is faster". Senior: it trades copies for correctness burden and coupling, so default to sockets (reversible, location-transparent) and move to shared memory only after profiling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that started with shared-memory queues between two services were stuck when one had to move to another host; sockets would have moved with a config change.

questions.promptHtml: What is a signal, and what is the difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL? Why does it matter in a rolling deploy?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Graceful shutdown is a daily senior concern; the answer separates people who have operated services from those who haven't.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A signal is an asynchronous notification with a number but no payload. SIGTERM (15) is a polite request: the process can catch it, drain in-flight requests and exit. SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught or ignored; the kernel just removes the process. In Kubernetes the kubelet sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 s default), then SIGKILL. If my app ignores SIGTERM I drop requests or get force-killed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each signal has a default action: terminate, core dump, stop, or ignore. A process can install a handler (except for SIGKILL and SIGSTOP). Handlers must be async-signal-safe: usually just set a flag or write a byte to a self-pipe, and the main loop does the real shutdown.

SIGHUP 1 reload config   SIGINT 2 Ctrl-C   SIGQUIT 3 thread dump (JVM)
SIGKILL 9 uncatchable    SIGTERM 15 graceful   SIGSTOP 19 uncatchable pause
Exit status: 143 = 128+15 (SIGTERM), 137 = 128+9 (SIGKILL, often OOM)
import signal, sys
def stop(signum, frame):
    sys.exit(0)           # real code: stop accepting, drain, flush, then exit
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, stop)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing you can catch SIGKILL.
  • Doing heavy work (malloc, printf, locks) inside a handler.
  • CMD ./start.sh in a Dockerfile: the shell is PID 1 and does not forward SIGTERM to the JVM child; use exec java ....

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does exit code 137 tell you? -> SIGKILL: OOM killer or grace period expired; check dmesg and pod events.
  2. How does a server reload config without downtime? -> SIGHUP handler re-reads config (nginx does this).
  3. Why can't you rely on SIGTERM for data safety? -> Power loss, OOM and SIGKILL skip it; durability needs fsync/WAL.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "TERM is graceful, KILL is forced". Senior adds PID 1 forwarding, grace-period tuning versus drain time, readiness-probe removal before SIGTERM, and reading exit codes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Java pod always took exactly 30 s to stop because the entrypoint script swallowed SIGTERM; deploys dropped in-flight requests until exec was added.

questions.contextHtml:
A nightly job shells out to a media converter and has started hanging for hours on a few large files; small files work. CPU is idle. The code:

import subprocess

def convert(path):
    p = subprocess.Popen(["ffconv", path, "-"],
                         stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)
    p.wait()                       # wait for it to finish
    return p.stdout.read()
$ ls -l /proc/<converter pid>/fd | grep pipe
l-wx------ 1 app app 64 1 -> pipe:[88231]
l-wx------ 1 app app 64 2 -> pipe:[88232]
$ cat /proc/<converter pid>/wchan
pipe_write

Failing inputs are all above ~60 KB of output. Disk space is fine, and the converter works when run by hand.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why only large outputs hang, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The converter is slow, add a timeout" or "increase CPU". It misses that both processes are blocked on each other and never looks at wchan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the converter write to stderr heavily? (A full stderr pipe blocks it too.) Is the hang size-dependent? (Yes, so a fixed buffer is involved.) Python version and is output streamed or buffered?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Kill the hung converter (kill -TERM), re-queue the file, and add timeout around the job so one hang does not block the whole batch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) pipe buffer full and nobody reading; (b) converter deadlocked internally; (c) disk or network stall; (d) zombie not reaped. pipe_write in wchan and the 60 KB threshold point to (a).
  4. How I'd verify: cat /proc/<pid>/wchan shows pipe_write; ls -l /proc/<parent>/fd shows the parent is in wait4; strace -p <converter> shows a write(1, ...) that never returns.
  5. Root cause: The parent calls wait() before reading. The converter fills the 64 KB stdout pipe and blocks in write. The parent waits for exit, the child waits for a reader: classic deadlock. Small outputs fit in the buffer, so they pass.
  6. Fix: Short term: use communicate(), which reads stdout and stderr concurrently. Long term: stream to a temp file or process chunks, and set a timeout.
def convert(path):
    p = subprocess.run(["ffconv", path, "-"], capture_output=True, timeout=600, check=True)
    return p.stdout          # for huge outputs: stdout=open(tmp, "wb") instead of a pipe
  1. Prevention: Lint rule/code review flag: never wait() on a Popen with PIPE before draining. Add a test with a 1 MB output. Alert on job duration.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not enlarge the pipe with F_SETPIPE_SZ as a fix; it only moves the threshold. I would not set stderr=PIPE and ignore it, which recreates the bug with the second pipe.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if output is 20 GB? -> Do not buffer in memory; redirect to a file or process in a streaming loop.
  • Java equivalent? -> ProcessBuilder: read stdout and stderr on separate threads, or redirectErrorStream(true) and drain one stream.
  • Why does communicate() not deadlock? -> It uses threads or select/poll to drain both pipes at once.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A report generator hung every month-end only: output crossed the pipe buffer for the biggest customer. Everyone suspected the database for two days; one cat wchan ended it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests timeouts or more CPU, cannot explain size dependence.
  • Hire: Identifies wait-before-read deadlock and uses communicate().
  • Strong hire: Also covers stderr pipe, wchan verification, streaming to file for huge outputs, and a regression test.

questions.promptHtml: How does a server handle 50,000 concurrent TCP connections on a few threads, and what pitfalls come with reading from TCP sockets?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes understanding of non-blocking I/O, epoll and the stream (not message) nature of TCP, all behind Nginx, Redis and Netty.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I make sockets non-blocking and register them with epoll; one thread calls epoll_wait, gets the list of ready sockets, and reads or writes until EAGAIN. That avoids a thread per connection. The pitfalls: TCP is a byte stream, so a recv can return half a message or two, so I need framing such as a length prefix; with edge-triggered epoll I must drain until EAGAIN; and every socket costs a file descriptor, so ulimit -n must be raised.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Server lifecycle: socket, bind, listen(backlog), accept, then read/write. Each socket has kernel send and receive buffers. With a blocking socket a slow client holds a thread; with 50,000 clients that is 50,000 stacks and heavy context switching. With epoll the kernel keeps a ready list, so cost scales with active connections, not total.

  • Level-triggered: epoll reports while data remains; forgiving.
  • Edge-triggered: reports once per new arrival; if I read part and stop, I never hear about the rest.
loop:
  n = epoll_wait(ep, events, 1024, -1)
  for each ready fd:
     if listener: accept until EAGAIN, set non-blocking, epoll_ctl ADD
     else: read until EAGAIN, parse frames [4-byte len][payload], handle partials
           write; if EAGAIN keep remaining bytes and wait for EPOLLOUT

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming one send equals one recv.
  • Running CPU-heavy work on the epoll thread so all connections stall.
  • Ignoring partial writes in non-blocking mode.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not select? -> O(n) scan per call and the 1024 fd limit; epoll is O(ready).
  2. What does Recv-Q mean on a listening socket in ss -lnt? -> Current accept-queue depth.
  3. How do you scale across cores? -> One epoll loop per core with SO_REUSEPORT or an acceptor handing off, like Nginx workers and Netty event loops.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use epoll or a thread pool". Senior adds edge vs level, framing, write backpressure, fd limits, SO_REUSEPORT, and keeping handlers off the I/O thread.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A gateway built on a blocking thread-per-connection model fell over at about 8k connections from thread stacks and scheduler overhead; the rewrite on an event loop handled 10x with a quarter of the CPUs.

questions.contextHtml:
A Java service on Kubernetes (30 pods) drops about 0.5% of requests on every deploy. Rolling update, terminationGracePeriodSeconds is the default. Pods show:

$ kubectl describe pod orders-7d9f | grep -A4 'Last State'
    Last State:  Terminated
      Reason:    Error
      Exit Code: 137
$ kubectl get events | grep orders-7d9f
Killing: Stopping container orders   (30s later) container did not terminate in time

Dockerfile: CMD ./start.sh. start.sh runs some env setup and then java -jar app.jar. The app has a JVM shutdown hook that drains the HTTP server in about 5 s. A teammate says "memory leak, exit 137 is OOM". dmesg on the node shows no OOM kills.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is happening and how you would fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts "137 means OOM" and starts tuning heap, or just raises the grace period without asking why the hook never ran.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the shutdown hook log line ever printed? Is the load balancer endpoint removed before SIGTERM? What is PID 1 in the container? Any preStop hook?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a preStop sleep of 5 to 10 s so endpoints are removed from the Service first, and raise the grace period to give headroom; this reduces drops while I fix root cause.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) SIGTERM never reaches the JVM because PID 1 is sh; (b) JVM got it but drain exceeds grace; (c) traffic still routed to a terminating pod; (d) real OOM. No OOM events in dmesg and the 30 s gap before 137 rule (d) out.
  4. How I'd verify: kubectl exec ... -- ps -ef shows PID 1 = /bin/sh ./start.sh, java is PID 7; kubectl logs lacks the hook line; strace -p 1 -e trace=signal or docker kill -s TERM locally to reproduce.
  5. Root cause: The shell as PID 1 receives SIGTERM, has no handler, and (as init) ignores signals without a handler. Java never hears it, so after 30 s the kubelet sends SIGKILL (137). Connections are cut mid-request.
  6. Fix: Short term: exec java -jar app.jar in start.sh (the process replaces the shell and becomes PID 1), or use ENTRYPOINT ["java", ...] exec form. Long term: add a tiny init (tini/--init) and a readiness flip on shutdown.
#!/bin/sh
export JAVA_OPTS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70"
exec java $JAVA_OPTS -jar app.jar   # exec: JVM becomes PID 1 and receives SIGTERM
  1. Prevention: CI test that sends SIGTERM to the container and asserts exit code 143 within N seconds; deploy dashboard for 5xx during rollout; lint Dockerfiles for shell-form CMD.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not just raising the grace period (hides the bug and slows deploys). Not trap hacks in the shell when exec is simpler. A preStop sleep is a pragmatic fix, not a design.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the app is Python behind gunicorn? -> SIGTERM goes to the master; confirm workers drain with graceful_timeout.
  • What if drain takes 45 s? -> Raise the grace period above drain time plus preStop and shorten client timeouts.
  • Why does PID 1 behave specially? -> The kernel does not apply default signal actions to init in a PID namespace, so it must handle signals explicitly.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments team chased 'random 502s on deploy' for a month; every pod took exactly 30.0 s to die. One ps -ef inside the container showed sh as PID 1.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Accepts the OOM theory or only increases timeouts.
  • Hire: Finds shell-as-PID-1, uses exec, explains 137.
  • Strong hire: Adds endpoint-removal race, preStop, init process, SIGTERM test in CI.

questions.contextHtml:
Two processes share a queue in a POSIX shared memory segment for a market-data feed (200k msgs/s). It works in tests, but in production the consumer occasionally crashes with SIGSEGV or reads garbage prices a few times a day.

struct Msg { double price; int qty; };
struct Shared {
    Msg* head;        // pointer to the next message slot
    int  count;
    Msg  slots[4096];
};
// Producer
Shared* s = (Shared*)mmap(nullptr, sizeof(Shared), PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE,
                          MAP_SHARED, fd, 0);
s->head = &s->slots[s->count % 4096];
s->head->price = p; s->head->qty = q;
s->count++;                       // consumer polls count
// Consumer (separate process, own mmap of the same fd)
while (last < s->count) { use(*s->head); last++; }

Both run on x86 with 8 cores. The segment is created by the producer with shm_open and ftruncate.
questions.promptHtml: List what is wrong and how you would fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a mutex around it" without noticing the stored pointer, or blaming the network.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Single producer, single consumer? Can the producer restart while the consumer runs? Is the ring bounded (what happens when the consumer is slow)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart both processes together and recreate the segment, and pause trading on mismatch via a checksum on each message, to stop bad prices flowing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) raw pointer stored in shared memory; (b) data race / torn reads with no atomics or memory ordering; (c) no overflow check, consumer lapped; (d) stale segment after producer restart.
  4. How I'd verify: Print s in both processes (different addresses); check the pointer value in /proc/<pid>/maps ranges; run with ThreadSanitizer-style stress test; ls -l /dev/shm for stale segments.
  5. Root cause: head holds a virtual address valid only in the producer; the consumer maps the segment at a different address, so *s->head dereferences garbage or an unmapped page (SIGSEGV). Separately, count++ is plain, not atomic or release-ordered, so the consumer can see the new count before the slot data, which gives torn or stale reads.
  6. Fix: Use indices, not pointers, and a single-producer single-consumer ring with atomics.
struct Shared {
    std::atomic<uint64_t> write_idx{0};   // producer only writes
    std::atomic<uint64_t> read_idx{0};    // consumer only writes
    Msg slots[4096];
};
// producer
auto w = s->write_idx.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
if (w - s->read_idx.load(std::memory_order_acquire) == 4096) { /* full: back off */ }
s->slots[w % 4096] = {p, q};
s->write_idx.store(w + 1, std::memory_order_release);   // publish after data
  1. Prevention: Rule: no pointers in shared memory, only offsets. Stress tests with different mapping addresses (ASLR on). Version/magic header and heartbeat for restart detection.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A process-shared mutex is simpler but adds latency and a dead-lock risk if the holder dies (use robust mutexes). I would not use volatile as a substitute for atomics.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Multiple producers? -> Need CAS-based slot claiming or per-producer rings; far trickier.
  • Producer crashes mid-write? -> Sequence number per slot (seqlock style) so the consumer can detect incomplete data.
  • Why is this fine on x86 only by luck? -> x86's strong ordering hides some bugs; ARM exposes them.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A feed handler ran for months on one box, then crashed after being moved to a host with a different ASLR layout order; the stored pointer had always 'worked' because both processes happened to map at the same address.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Only says add a lock, misses the pointer.
  • Hire: Spots pointer-in-shared-memory and missing atomics.
  • Strong hire: Delivers SPSC ring with acquire/release, overflow handling, and restart/crash recovery.

questions.subtopic: POSIX shared memory setup and pitfalls
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through how two unrelated processes share memory on Linux, and what operational pitfalls come with it.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the real API sequence and the leaks, limits and container issues that bite in production.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: One process calls shm_open("/name"), which creates a file under /dev/shm (a tmpfs), then ftruncate to set the size; every process then mmaps it with MAP_SHARED. After that they read and write the same physical pages with no syscalls. I add a process-shared mutex or semaphore, or a lock-free ring. Pitfalls: segments outlive the process so they leak, Docker caps /dev/shm at 64 MB by default, and the memory counts toward the cgroup limit.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A: fd = shm_open("/feed", O_CREAT|O_RDWR, 0600); ftruncate(fd, 1<<20); p = mmap(.. MAP_SHARED, fd, 0)
B: fd = shm_open("/feed", O_RDWR, 0);                                  p = mmap(.. MAP_SHARED, fd, 0)
Cleanup: shm_unlink("/feed")  (name removed; pages freed when last mapping goes away)

Alternatives: SysV shmget/shmat (see ipcs -m), file-backed MAP_SHARED mmap (persists to disk), and anonymous MAP_SHARED before fork.

Synchronisation options: pthread_mutexattr_setpshared with the mutex placed in the segment (use the robust attribute so a crash of the holder does not wedge everyone), sem_open, or atomics. Each process maps at a different virtual address so only offsets may be stored, never pointers.

Failure detection is on me: a dead peer does not produce EOF, so I add a heartbeat timestamp or use pidfd/kill(pid, 0) checks.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting shm_unlink, leaving garbage in /dev/shm after crashes.
  • Docker default 64 MB /dev/shm: use --shm-size or mount an emptyDir with medium: Memory (counted against the pod limit).
  • Believing shared memory is free of the memory limit: it is charged to the cgroup.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you see what exists? -> ls -l /dev/shm, ipcs -m, lsof /dev/shm/*.
  2. What if the lock holder dies? -> Robust mutexes return EOWNERDEAD; the next locker repairs state.
  3. How would you notify the consumer without polling? -> A futex/eventfd or a small socket/pipe doorbell, keeping bulk data in shared memory.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "mmap shared region". Senior covers the full lifecycle, robust locking, offsets not pointers, cgroup accounting, /dev/shm sizing and dead-peer detection.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Headless Chrome crashed randomly in CI containers ("Aw, Snap") until --shm-size=1g was set, because renderer buffers overran the 64 MB tmpfs.

questions.contextHtml:
An API gateway (Java, 4 cores, 8 GB) starts failing at 14:10 with "Too many open files" and refused connections while CPU is 20% and memory is fine. Traffic is normal, 1,800 rps. On the box:

$ ulimit -n  (inside the service's systemd unit)
1024
$ ls /proc/4410/fd | wc -l
1021
$ ss -tan | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c
   88 ESTAB
  903 CLOSE-WAIT
   20 TIME-WAIT

A deploy of the gateway went out at 13:40 with a new upstream HTTP client. A teammate wants to raise the thread pool from 200 to 800. Another says it's a DDoS because there are many connections.
questions.promptHtml: What is going on, how do you stop it now, and how do you stop it recurring?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Raises ulimit and the thread pool and calls it done, or blames a DDoS with no evidence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which side holds the CLOSE-WAIT sockets (upstream or client)? Did the count grow steadily since 13:40? Does the new client library reuse connections?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the 13:40 deploy (or restart pods one at a time, behind the LB) to clear leaked sockets; raise LimitNOFILE as a safety net, not as the fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) application not closing responses/connections (CLOSE-WAIT = peer closed, we did not); (b) ulimit too low for legitimate concurrency; (c) DDoS; (d) TIME-WAIT buildup. The state counts (903 CLOSE-WAIT, only 88 ESTAB) point firmly to (a).
  4. How I'd verify: ss -tanp state close-wait to see the remote ports and owning fds; lsof -p 4410 | grep CLOSE_WAIT | awk '{print $9}' | sort | uniq -c to see which upstream; heap dump or thread dump to find unclosed responses; graph fd count versus time.
  5. Root cause: CLOSE-WAIT means the remote side sent FIN and the kernel is waiting for the application to call close(). The new client leaks connections when a response body is not consumed or closed (e.g., an error path skips close). Each leak holds an fd until the 1024 limit.
  6. Fix: Short term: rollback/restart and raise LimitNOFILE=65535 in the unit. Long term: fix with try-with-resources on every response, a bounded connection pool with idle timeouts, and keep-alive.
client.newCall(req).execute().use { resp ->   // use{} always closes the body
    handle(resp)
}
  1. Prevention: Alert on process_open_fds / limit > 0.7 and on CLOSE-WAIT count; load test with error paths; client library wrapper that enforces closing.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not just a bigger thread pool (more threads, same leak). Not tuning TCP sysctls (tcp_tw_reuse) because TIME-WAIT is not the problem. A higher fd limit only delays the crash.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the states were TIME-WAIT 28,000? -> Short-lived connections: add keep-alive/pooling, widen ephemeral ports, rarely tune tcp_tw_reuse.
  • What if it was a real DDoS? -> Would show ESTAB or SYN-RECV from many sources, with rate limiting at the edge.
  • Why does the app not get an error on a CLOSE-WAIT socket? -> It only sees EOF on the next read; if it never reads, nothing tells it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A leak only on the 429 path: the rate-limited branch returned early without closing the body; it took weeks of normal traffic to hit 1024 and failed on a Monday morning peak.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Raises limits and threads, accepts the DDoS theory.
  • Hire: Reads CLOSE-WAIT correctly and finds the unclosed connection.
  • Strong hire: Adds fd alerting, pooling policy, the rollback-first stance and verifies with ss/lsof.

questions.contextHtml: You are designing a host-level agent (a sidecar) that collects metrics from 40 application processes on the same machine. Each app emits roughly 5,000 small events per second (100 bytes each) and occasionally a 20 MB profile dump. Requirements: the agent must tell when an app has died, an app must never be blocked or slowed by a slow agent, apps are written in Java, Go and Python, and some apps are in containers while the agent runs on the host. The security team wants only the right users to be able to connect.
questions.promptHtml: Which IPC mechanism(s) do you choose and why? What would make you change your mind?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Shared memory, it is fastest." Ignores cross-language support, containers, security, and failure detection.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is loss of an event acceptable under pressure? Is latency important or just throughput? 200k events/s total at 100 bytes is only 20 MB/s: is that the real load? Are apps containers sharing a mount namespace with the host socket path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (Design question) The first move is to define the failure rule: apps drop events rather than block.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Candidates: (a) Unix domain socket (datagram or stream); (b) TCP/gRPC on localhost; (c) shared memory ring per app; (d) pipes/FIFOs; (e) files plus tail.
  4. How I'd verify: Prototype with a benchmark: 40 clients x 5k events/s, measure p99 send latency and CPU with perf/strace -c. Test agent stall: does the app's send block?
  5. Root cause (reasoning): 20 MB/s is trivial for a Unix socket (copies are cheap; expect single-digit microseconds per send). Shared memory's benefits only matter at several GB/s or microsecond budgets and it needs per-language ring code and heartbeats. A Unix domain socket gives: every language has a client; SO_PEERCRED lets the agent verify the UID/PID of the connecting process; file-permission access control on the path; the container can bind-mount the socket path; and peer death shows up as EOF/reset on the agent side.
  6. Fix (decision): Use a Unix domain socket (SOCK_STREAM with a length-prefixed frame, or SOCK_SEQPACKET for message boundaries). Non-blocking sends with a small bounded buffer in the app: if EAGAIN, drop and count. For the 20 MB dumps, send a file path (written to a shared directory or via memfd and SCM_RIGHTS fd passing) instead of streaming through the socket.
  7. Prevention: Metrics on dropped events, connection counts and agent queue depth; version field in the frame; chaos test that SIGSTOPs the agent and checks the app's p99 is unchanged.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not TCP localhost (works, but a few tens of microseconds more per call, port management, and weaker peer identity). Not pipes (one-way, hard to multiplex). Not shared memory first. I'd switch to a shared-memory ring only if profiling shows the socket path costs more than about 5% of app CPU, or if rates reach millions of events/s.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The agent moves to a remote collector? -> The framing and protocol stay; swap AF_UNIX for TCP/gRPC with TLS.
  • An app hangs but stays alive? -> Socket liveness is not app health; add periodic heartbeat events.
  • Windows apps appear? -> Named pipes or localhost TCP; keep the protocol transport-agnostic.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team built a clever shared-memory metrics pipe; two years later nobody could add a Python client without a C extension, and a crashed app left the lock held. They replaced it with a Unix socket and lost nothing measurable.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Picks shared memory for speed, no requirements questions.
  • Hire: Picks Unix sockets with reasons (cross-language, peer creds, failure detection).
  • Strong hire: Quantifies load, specifies drop-not-block, handles big payloads via fd passing, and states switch conditions.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't you call printf or malloc in a signal handler, and how do you write signal handling for a multithreaded daemon correctly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Signal bugs are rare, subtle and nasty; this separates people who have read the man pages from those who have not.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A handler can interrupt the program at any instruction, including inside malloc or printf holding an internal lock. If the handler calls the same function, it deadlocks or corrupts state. So handlers may only call async-signal-safe functions, in practice setting a volatile sig_atomic_t flag or write()ing a byte to a self-pipe. For a multithreaded daemon I block signals in all worker threads and dedicate one thread to sigwait, so signals become ordinary events.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rules to remember:

  • Only functions on the POSIX async-signal-safe list (write, _exit, kill, sem_post...) are allowed. malloc, printf, pthread_mutex_lock are not.
  • Standard signals do not queue: three SIGCHLD arriving quickly may be delivered once, so the handler/loop must call waitpid(-1, WNOHANG) until it returns 0. Real-time signals do queue.
  • Signals interrupt blocking syscalls, returning EINTR (or restarting if SA_RESTART). Code must handle EINTR.
  • In a multithreaded process a process-directed signal goes to any thread that has not blocked it.
  • Use sigaction, not signal, for portable semantics.
sigset_t set; sigemptyset(&set);
sigaddset(&set, SIGTERM); sigaddset(&set, SIGHUP);
pthread_sigmask(SIG_BLOCK, &set, nullptr);      // block before creating threads
std::thread sig([&]{
    int s; sigwait(&set, &s);                    // synchronous, no handler restrictions
    if (s == SIGTERM) begin_shutdown();
    if (s == SIGHUP)  reload_config();
});

Modern alternatives: signalfd (signals as a readable fd in epoll) and pidfd for children.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Logging from a handler (printf or a logging library with locks).
  • Assuming each signal is delivered: they coalesce.
  • Not blocking signals before creating threads, so any thread runs the handler.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the self-pipe trick? -> The handler writes a byte to a pipe whose read end is in the event loop, converting the signal into an I/O event.
  2. What happens to zombie children if SIGCHLD is ignored? -> With SIG_IGN (or SA_NOCLDWAIT) children are reaped automatically.
  3. Why is SIGSEGV handling dangerous? -> Returning re-executes the faulting instruction; you can only log with safe calls and exit, or use sigsetjmp-style recovery in very special cases.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "don't do much in handlers". Senior knows the safe list, coalescing, EINTR/SA_RESTART, the dedicated sigwait thread and signalfd.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A daemon deadlocked once a month: a SIGHUP handler called syslog while the main thread held the logging lock. Moving to a flag plus event loop removed it.

questions.contextHtml:
A Go API behind an L4 load balancer handles 25k rps across 12 nodes. During a marketing push (3x traffic in 2 minutes) clients see connect timeouts of 1 s, 3 s, 7 s, but the app's own latency graphs look normal and CPU is 45%. One node:

$ ss -lnt sport = :8080
State   Recv-Q  Send-Q  Local Address:Port
LISTEN  129     128     0.0.0.0:8080
$ nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows TcpExtListenDrops
TcpExtListenOverflows           48213    0.0
TcpExtListenDrops               48213    0.0
$ sysctl net.core.somaxconn
net.core.somaxconn = 128

The service calls net.Listen (Go uses somaxconn as the backlog). The LB health checks still pass. Someone suggests adding more pods; someone else suspects packet loss in the network.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose this and propose fixes in order.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more nodes / blame network" with no explanation of why app latency looks fine while clients time out.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Kernel version (older kernels use a SYN backlog separately)? Is the accept loop CPU-bound or blocked? Did GC pauses or a lock stall accepts? Do timeouts match SYN retransmit schedule (1 s, 3 s, 7 s)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise net.core.somaxconn (e.g., 4096) and restart or re-listen so the new backlog applies, and scale out nodes if CPU allows. Both are quick, reversible.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) accept queue overflow: Recv-Q 129 against Send-Q 128 and rising ListenOverflows; (b) SYN flood/syncookies; (c) network loss; (d) conntrack table full; (e) accept thread starved. The 1 s, 3 s, 7 s pattern equals SYN retransmits after dropped final ACK/SYN.
  4. How I'd verify: ss -lnt repeatedly during the spike (Recv-Q near Send-Q); nstat deltas; dmesg | grep -i 'SYN flooding'; conntrack -S; tcpdump -ni eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0 and port 8080' showing SYN retransmits; check app accept rate with strace -c -e accept4.
  5. Root cause: The kernel keeps completed handshakes in an accept queue of size min(backlog, somaxconn) = 128. During the burst, connections arrive faster than the app calls accept in short bursts (stop-the-world or a busy loop). When the queue is full the kernel drops the handshake ACK; the client retries SYN with exponential backoff, which is exactly the 1/3/7 s timeouts. The app never sees these connections so its latency graphs look fine, a classic red herring.
  6. Fix: Short term: sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=4096, restart service to apply the larger backlog; also tcp_max_syn_backlog. Long term: dedicated accept goroutine/loop that never blocks, SO_REUSEPORT listeners per core, autoscale before the push, and LB-side connection limits with queueing.
sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=4096
echo 'net.core.somaxconn=4096' > /etc/sysctl.d/90-backlog.conf
  1. Prevention: Alert on ListenOverflows rate and accept-queue depth; load test with burst profiles; capacity review before campaigns.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A huge backlog only buffers delay: clients still wait; it hides overload and increases latency under sustained excess. Not adding tcp_abort_on_overflow=1 (resets users instead of retrying). Not blaming the network before reading counters.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did restart matter? -> Backlog is fixed at listen() time; changing sysctl does not resize existing queues.
  • What if ListenOverflows is zero but connects still time out? -> Look at SYN queue/syncookies, conntrack or LB limits.
  • Could HTTP keep-alive help? -> Fewer new connections per request, cutting handshake pressure.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Every Black Friday-style spike showed 'healthy' dashboards and angry users. The turning point was graphing ListenOverflows, a counter nobody had ever charted.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Scales out and suspects the network blindly.
  • Hire: Identifies accept-queue overflow from ss and nstat, raises somaxconn.
  • Strong hire: Explains SYN retransmit timing, restart requirement, accept-loop health, alerting and the trade-off of deeper queues.

questions.contextHtml:
A feed-normalisation service passes quotes from a network-receiver process to 6 strategy processes on one 32-core host via local TCP sockets. Today it moves 300k msgs/s (64 bytes) with p99 latency of 180 microseconds, CPU in kernel networking about 30%. The business expects 3M msgs/s and wants p99 under 20 microseconds. Profile:

$ perf top -p <receiver>
  18.2%  [kernel] tcp_sendmsg
  11.5%  [kernel] __copy_user
   9.7%  [kernel] tcp_write_xmit
   7.0%  [kernel] sock_def_readable
$ strace -c -p <receiver>   (5 s)
% time  calls    syscall
 71.2%  1.4M     sendto

Strategies only read; each needs every message. The team proposes Kafka, "since it scales".
questions.promptHtml: How would you re-architect for 10x throughput and 9x lower latency? What new risks appear?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Kafka" or "just add cores"; neither addresses per-message syscalls and copies nor the 20 microsecond target.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must messages be durable or is loss on crash ok? Strict ordering? Can a slow strategy be allowed to miss data (drop/gap) or must it back-pressure the receiver? Same NUMA node?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Short term, batch messages into one sendmsg and disable Nagle to cut syscalls, buying maybe 3x while the real fix is built.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The time goes to per-message syscalls, TCP stack work and copies: 1.4M sendto calls/s. At 3M msgs/s even batching will not reach 20 microseconds. Kafka adds network and disk hops, so it cannot reach 20 microseconds p99.
  4. How I'd verify: Prototype a shared-memory SPSC/broadcast ring and benchmark message rate and p99 with rdtsc timestamps; perf stat for cache misses; check numactl --hardware.
  5. Root cause: Message passing costs a syscall and two copies per message per consumer: here 6 x 300k = 1.8M sends/s, growing to 18M. The fix is to remove the kernel from the data path.
  6. Fix: One shared-memory ring (shm_open plus mmap, huge pages if possible): the receiver writes each message once; each strategy keeps its own read cursor (Disruptor/Aeron-style broadcast). Cache-line-aligned slots, sequence numbers per slot, busy-spin readers pinned to cores, memory fences (acquire/release). Slow consumers are detected by lag and either skipped with a gap marker or fed from a snapshot. Keep Kafka off the hot path, and use it only for asynchronous persistence by a separate consumer.
 receiver --write once--> [ ring of 64B-aligned slots, seq per slot ]
                              ^cursor A  ^cursor B ... ^cursor F  (each consumer private)
  1. Prevention: Metrics on lag per consumer and ring wrap events; a heartbeat slot so consumers detect a dead receiver; replay test after crash; versioned slot layout; /dev/shm and cgroup sizing checks.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Shared memory ties all processes to one host and one team's discipline (no pointers, strict layout, crash recovery). Busy-spinning burns cores. I would not do it before proving sockets cannot meet the target, and I would keep a socket fallback for remote or non-latency-critical consumers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A strategy needs to run on another host? -> Bridge process reading the ring and publishing over multicast/Aeron; keep the hot path local.
  • A strategy crashes mid-read? -> Cursors are private, so others are unaffected; on restart it resumes from the latest sequence.
  • Why not one ring per consumer? -> Costs 6 writes per message; a single ring with N cursors writes once.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A latency-critical pipeline went from 150 to 8 microseconds p99 by replacing loopback TCP with a broadcast ring; the next outage was a producer restart that republished sequence numbers from zero, which consumers read as 'old data'.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests Kafka/more cores, ignores syscall and copy costs.
  • Hire: Proposes shared memory ring with atomics and consumer cursors.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies syscall rates, defines slow-consumer and crash semantics, keeps persistence off the hot path, and names the coupling risks.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review. A video-processing service has an ingest process and 4 encoder workers sharing frames via a POSIX shm segment guarded by a process-shared pthread mutex. At 03:20 an encoder was OOM-killed (dmesg: Killed process 9120 (encoder)). From then on all workers hung and the ingest process stopped; the pipeline was dead for 4 hours until a human restarted things. After restart, the new instance failed with "cannot allocate memory" even though the host had 20 GB free.

$ ls -l /dev/shm
-rw------- 1 svc svc 1073741824 Nov 10 03:01 frames        <- 1 GB, old
-rw------- 1 svc svc 1073741824 Nov 10 07:20 frames.1
...  (9 files, total 9 GB; /dev/shm is a 16 GB tmpfs)
$ cat /proc/<ingest>/wchan
futex_wait_queue

There was no alert; the process was alive, the container healthy.
questions.promptHtml: Reconstruct the failure, and say what you would change in design, operations and monitoring.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add auto-restart" only. It misses the held mutex, the missing liveness signal and the segment leak.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the mutex created with the robust attribute? Does anything call shm_unlink at shutdown? Is the ingest-to-encoder flow back-pressured, so one dead consumer stops everything? What do health checks test?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Kill remaining workers, shm_unlink/remove stale files, restart in order, and confirm free /dev/shm. Adding a temporary external watchdog that restarts the group on stall.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the OOM-killed encoder held the process-shared mutex, so everyone blocked on futex_wait forever; (b) the ingest ring was full because a dead consumer never advanced its cursor; (c) the segments leaked on each restart so tmpfs filled; (d) health checks only test process liveness.
  4. How I'd verify: wchan = futex_wait_queue on all processes confirms a lock wait; read the mutex owner TID (glibc stores it) and check that the TID no longer exists; ls /dev/shm and df -h /dev/shm for leaks; check dmesg for the kill timestamp (03:20) matching the stall.
  5. Root cause: A SIGKILL'd process cannot release locks. A non-robust process-shared mutex stays locked forever, so a single death turned into a total outage. Every restart created a new 1 GB frames.N segment without unlinking the old, so tmpfs (counted as memory) shrank until allocation failed despite free RAM elsewhere. And liveness checks measured "process exists", not "frames are flowing".
  6. Fix: Use PTHREAD_MUTEX_ROBUST (the next locker gets EOWNERDEAD, repairs state and calls pthread_mutex_consistent), or better, lock-free per-worker queues so no lock can be held by a dead process. Use a supervisor that treats any worker death as a group restart, shm_unlink at startup and in a cleanup hook, and a single well-known segment name with a generation number inside.
  7. Prevention: Heartbeat counter each worker increments; a watchdog alerts if frames-processed-per-minute drops to 0; liveness probe on throughput not PID; alert on /dev/shm usage above 70%; chaos test with kill -9 on each role monthly; set cgroup memory so encoders are not OOM-killed first.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Robust mutexes add complexity and still need state repair logic. Not "just bigger /dev/shm". Not silently ignoring EOWNERDEAD. If per-frame durability matters, accept that shared memory is volatile and have an upstream replay source.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did the container look healthy? -> Probes checked HTTP on a thread that did not touch the lock.
  • Could kill(pid,0) in a monitor suffice? -> Detects death, not hangs; combine with throughput metrics.
  • Does the OOM kill also affect the page accounting of the segment? -> shm pages remain charged to the cgroup until unlinked and all mappings close.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A pipeline outage lasted 4 hours simply because 'the process is up' was the only health signal. After the review the single most valuable change was a throughput-based liveness probe, not any locking change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Proposes auto-restart and nothing else.
  • Hire: Identifies the dead lock holder and the leaked segments, with robust mutex fix.
  • Strong hire: Adds throughput-based liveness, group-restart policy, chaos testing, cgroup accounting and replay semantics.
